MT103.name: Single Customer Credit Transfer
MT103.note: The highest-volume migration in the industry. One MT103 becomes one pacs.008, but the party fields fan out from single tags into structured name, address and account elements — which is why address data quality dominates MT103 migration projects.

fields.note: Also commonly mapped to CdtTrfTxInf.PmtId.InstrId, since MT had one reference where MX has several.
MT packed a code and a time into one tag; MX gives each timestamp its own element.
No MX counterpart. CRED was implied by the message type itself, so the information is redundant in ISO 20022.
Routes to InstrForNxtAgt instead when the instruction was aimed at an intermediary.
A domestic proprietary code. Only maps to Purp.Cd if it happens to be an ISO external purpose value.

fields.mtName: Value Date / Currency / Interbank Settled Amount
fields.note: One MT tag, three pieces of MX data. The currency becomes an attribute of the amount.

The hardest field in the migration. The option letter decided whether you got an account, a BIC or four lines of free text; MX wants a structured name, a structured address and a typed account identifier. Parsing legacy free-text addresses into StrtNm/TwnNm/Ctry is the bulk of the work.
Moves out of the payload and into the business application header.
Maps to SttlmAcct instead where the tag carried an account rather than an institution — the MT option letter is what disambiguates, and it is easy to lose.
A rename that misleads: 'account with institution' is simply the creditor's bank.
Same structural fan-out as field 50a.
MT allowed 4 lines of 35 characters, so 140 total. MX allows 140 per occurrence — but CBPR+ permits only one occurrence, so the capacity is unchanged despite appearances.
BEN maps to CRED, OUR to DEBT, SHA to SHAR. Not symmetric in reverse: SLEV has no MT equivalent at all.
MT had separate repeatable tags for sender's and receiver's charges; MX merges them into one repeating block where each entry names its charging agent.
In practice field 72 was a dumping ground of coded and uncoded text. Much of its real content belongs in properly typed MX elements, so a literal mapping preserves the mess.
Lived in the network header in MT; a first-class payload element in MX.
Structured remittance information is MX-only. Nothing in MT103 can carry invoice-level detail.

MT101.name: Request for Transfer
MT101.note: Customer-to-bank initiation. MT101's flat repeating sequences become pain.001's three-level nesting, which is a genuine gain — shared batch data stops being repeated per payment.

fields.note: MT101 split large files across messages with a manual index. pain.001 has no equivalent — you send one document, or several independent ones.
MT101 reused tag 50a for two different roles, distinguished only by position. A real source of mapping bugs.
No MX element. Authorisation moved out of the message into channel-level entitlements.
Moves up to batch level in MX, though it can still be set per transaction.
MX-only, and consequential: it decides whether the debtor's statement shows one lump debit or one entry per payment.

MT202.name: General Financial Institution Transfer
MT202.note: Bank-to-bank, no customer. A clean mapping because both messages carry institutions rather than parties.

fields.note: Becomes the Debtor, which is a financial institution in this message — not a party with a name and address.

MT202COV.name: General FI Transfer (Cover)
MT202COV.note: Same mapping as MT202 for sequence A, plus sequence B — the underlying customer credit transfer details — landing in UndrlygCstmrCdtTrf. The variant exists so the receiving agent can sanctions-screen the real parties behind a bank-to-bank cover payment.

fields.note: Identical to MT202.

MT205.name: Financial Institution Transfer Execution
MT205.note: Domestic equivalent of MT202, used within a single clearing system. Maps to the same pacs.009, with SettlementMethod normally CLRG rather than a correspondent arrangement.

MT204.name: Financial Markets Direct Debit
MT204.note: Collection between institutions. MT204's one-credit-many-debits layout survives in pacs.010's CdtInstr wrapper, which is unusual among the pacs messages.

MT104.name: Direct Debit and Request for Debit Transfer
MT104.note: Maps to pacs.003 for the interbank leg, or pain.008 when the sender is the creditor rather than its bank. Mandate data has no MT equivalent, so MT104 flows carried mandate evidence outside the message entirely. MT104 served both roles depending on who sent it, so it maps to pain.008 when the creditor sends it to its own bank and pacs.003 for the interbank leg.

fields.note: Mandate id and signature date are MX-only. Their absence from MT is why direct debit disputes were so hard to resolve from message data alone.

MT940.name: Customer Statement Message
MT940.note: The upgrade with the largest practical payoff. MT940's :61: statement line gave you a date, an amount, a two-letter type and free text; camt.053 gives structured parties, the payer's own reference, the UETR and itemised charges. Reconciliation rates move substantially.

fields.note: One MT tag carrying two numbers becomes two explicit elements.
MT used distinct tags per balance kind; MX uses one repeating Bal block with a type code. More uniform, but you must read the type.
The core transformation. Value date, entry date, debit/credit mark, amount, transaction type and reference were positional subfields of one tag; each becomes a named element.
MT's RC and RD reversal marks become CdtDbtInd plus RvslInd true — two elements where MT had one character.
A 4-character MT code becomes a three-level ISO classification plus an optional proprietary code.
34 characters of whatever survived the chain, versus a dedicated reference the payer set.
A literal mapping, but the point of migrating is to populate the structured elements instead of relaying narrative text.
Structured debtor and creditor on a statement entry are MX-only — in MT940 the payer's identity was whatever appeared in field 86.

MT950.name: Statement Message
MT950.note: The bank-to-bank statement. Same target as MT940 but typically carrying fewer details, since nostro reconciliation needs balances and amounts more than party data.

MT941.name: Balance Report
MT941.note: A balances-only intraday report. Maps to a camt.052 carrying Bal blocks and no entries.

fields.note: The as-at moment, which is the whole value of an intraday report.

MT942.name: Interim Transaction Report
MT942.note: Intraday activity since the last report. Maps to a camt.052 with entries that may still be PDNG.

fields.note: Only expressible in camt.060 as a request filter, not in the report itself. The report no longer tells you what threshold produced it.

MT900.name: Confirmation of Debit
MT900.note: A single debit confirmation. Maps to a camt.054 with CdtDbtInd set to DBIT.

fields.note: CdtDbtInd must be set to DBIT explicitly — in MT the message type itself carried the direction.

MT910.name: Confirmation of Credit
MT910.note: A single credit confirmation — the message a corporate waits on before releasing goods. Maps to a camt.054 with CdtDbtInd set to CRDT.

fields.note: Structured in MX, which is what lets an inbound credit be matched to a customer automatically.

MT920.name: Request Message
MT920.note: Asks for a statement or report. The MT message-type number being requested becomes an ISO message definition identifier.

fields.note: '940' becomes 'camt.053.001.08'. The version suffix is new and must be right.

MT192.name: Request for Cancellation
MT192.note: MT192 was largely free-format, with the original payment's details retyped into field 79 as text. camt.056 makes the whole request structured and machine-actionable, which is what made automated stop-and-recall possible.

fields.mtName: MT and Date of the Original Message
Narrative Description of the Original Message
fields.note: The big win. What was unparseable narrative becomes typed elements plus a coded cancellation reason.
A coded reason. MT192 had no reason code at all, so every request needed human reading.
A case identifier threaded through the whole exchange — MT had no case concept.

MT196.name: Answers
MT196.note: The reply to MT192. Field 76's answer codes become a typed confirmation status.

fields.mtName: MT and Date of the Original Message

fields.note: MT answer codes map onto CNCL, PDCR, RJCR and friends.

MT199.name: Free Format Message
MT199.note: MT199 was a single 35-line free-text field used for anything, status updates very much included. There is no field-level mapping, because there were no fields — pacs.002 replaces narrative prose with coded statuses and reasons. Any migration that maps MT199 text into AddtlInf has preserved the problem rather than solved it.

fields.note: Only a fallback. The status itself should be a TxSts code and the reason a StsRsn code.
A coded, machine-readable status. The entire reason the migration was worth doing.

MT299.name: Free Format Message (Treasury)
MT299.note: The treasury-category sibling of MT199, with the same lack of structure and the same replacement.

MT103RETN.name: Returned Customer Credit Transfer
MT103RETN.note: A returned MT103, marked by a /RETN/ code in field 72. pacs.004 makes the return a first-class message type with a coded reason, instead of a repurposed payment with a magic string in a narrative field.

fields.note: The whole return mechanism lived in a code word inside a free-text field. This is the clearest single example of why MT exception handling could not be automated.
Roles swap on a return: the original debtor becomes the creditor of the return.
